seats.name: seat-1
argv:
Read spec.txt (the STAMP language) and program.stamp. Determine exactly what the program outputs
when run under that specification.

Write your final answer, and only your final answer with no explanation, to a file named
answer.txt in your current working directory: the printed values in order, separated by single
spaces, on one line.

The room's final agreed proposal text must be exactly your answer and nothing else (no explanation) — that text is read as the submitted answer once the room concludes.

Join room rq1 as seat-1 (agent claude, expected_participants 3). Leave the room once it has concluded.
seats.text:
The room concluded on prop_60bd3082, and I've left it. `answer.txt` holds the agreed answer:

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`

I got this by tracing the program by hand against the spec; I didn't run it through an interpreter.

My first trace had the last two values as `101 5`. I was wrong there. Scope is per call, so `inner` can't see `outer`'s local `a` and reads global `a` = 0, which gives 100. That matches the other two seats' openings.

The verification gate's challenge requirement was only met by seat-2's challenge, which counted as non-blocking. My first challenge was recorded under seat-3's name because I left out my participant id.

seats.text:
The room reached agreement on the program's output, and I've written it to `answer.txt`. I then left the room. All three seats reached the same answer independently except for one value.

The answer is:

`105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5`

I traced the program by hand against the spec. I didn't run an interpreter, so the "verify" board entry I posted only records `wc -w answer.txt` (34 values) plus that hand trace. seat-1 posted their own entry under the same key.

seat-1's opening answer had 101 instead of 100 for `PRINT CALL outer 1`. The spec says a call reads its own locals, else the global. `inner` has no `a` of its own, so `a` reads as the global 0 rather than `outer`'s parameter, and the result is 0 + 100 = 100. seat-1 came around to 100 after that was pointed out.

The room accepted the proposal (prop_60bd3082) 3–0. seat-1's non-blocking challenge is listed as unresolved in the conclusion. It only restates the 100 reading.

seats.text:
The room agreed on the output, and I've written it to `answer.txt` and left the room. The vote was 3 of 3 in favour. I got the answer by tracing the program by hand against the spec, not by running an interpreter.

```
105 100 101 101 102 101 2432902008176640000 0 7 101 7 7 7 3 15 0 0 4 6 30 0 27 10 23 1 1 3 1267650600228229401496703205376 1 0 0 -3 100 5
```

Seat-1's opening answer had 101 for the second-to-last value instead of 100. They read `a` inside `inner` as seeing `outer`'s local. The spec's SCOPE rule says a read uses only the current call's locals, then the global. So `a` reads the never-assigned global, which is 0, and the result is 100. Seat-1 then agreed, though their challenge on that clause is still recorded as an unresolved objection on the conclusion.
